# Google Labs' Tabletop Lets Groups Plan Together in One Shared Space

> **In short:** Google Labs has introduced Tabletop, an experiment for planning with a group. You add links, files, and ideas, then ask the @tabletop assistant to build things like trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters, or tournament brackets. It's rolling out in the U.S. to adults 18 and up through a waitlist.

Anyone who has tried to plan a family trip over a group text knows the mess. Someone posts a restaurant link, someone else sends a spreadsheet, and the final plan lives in five different places. Google's new experiment, Tabletop, is an attempt to pull all of that into one space.

## What Tabletop is

Tabletop is a Google Labs experiment. A Labs project is a early-stage product that Google is testing with real people before deciding whether to keep it. That means features can change, and not everyone can use it yet.

The core idea is a shared workspace for a group. Google's Design and Engineering Lead for Google Labs, Roman Nurik, describes it as a place where everyone can pitch in, build, and decide together. Google says the tool is built for real-time collaboration, which means several people can work in the same space at the same moment.

## How the pieces fit together

Tabletop works through three main parts:

- **Your materials.** You add links, files, and ideas to the space. Think of this as your group's pile of research: the hotel you liked, the menu you saw online, the bracket rules your league uses.
- **The @tabletop prompt.** A prompt is simply the instruction you type to an AI tool. Here, you type @tabletop followed by what you want, such as a dinner poll for Saturday.
- **Starter templates.** If you don't know what to ask for, you can choose a ready-made template as your starting point instead.

Google lists four kinds of output: custom interactive trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters (tools that work out who owes whom after a shared bill), and tournament brackets. "Interactive" means people can respond inside the result, not just read it.

## Sharing it with the group

Once your space is ready, Google suggests dropping the invite link into your group chat. Anyone with the link can join and use the space at the same time, a bit like several people editing one shared document.

This is the part that makes Tabletop different from a single person's notes app. The plan isn't something you build alone and then forward. Everyone can add to it while it's happening.

## Getting access

Tabletop is rolling out in the U.S. for people 18 and older, and access is by waitlist. You can sign up at labs.google/tabletop. Google has not announced when everyone will get in, so check back there for updates rather than waiting on a date.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: If you organize a family trip, a potluck, or a weekend get-together, Tabletop could replace the scattered group-chat thread with one shared plan.
- **For your business or work**: Tabletop is aimed at personal and group coordination, so the announcement doesn't describe business uses. If you run a team event or club, you can still apply the same idea of collecting materials in one place.
- **If you're just getting started**: Sign up for the waitlist first. Then think about your next group event and list the links, files, and ideas you'd want in one place.
- **If you already use it**: Once you're in, add a shared file or list to your space and ask @tabletop for a tournament bracket or dinner poll based on it. Then share the invite link so everyone can respond at once.

## Wrap-up

Tabletop is Google's experiment in making group planning feel like one shared space instead of a pile of messages. You add your links, files, and ideas, use @tabletop or a starter template to build the plan, and share the invite link so everyone can join. Today, your next step is simple: go to labs.google/tabletop and join the waitlist, then pick the next group plan you're dreading and imagine it in one place.
